name: Bare Deictic Calendar NP
pattern: NP[this/last/next + calendar noun or weekday] in temporal adjunct use

entry.name: Bare Deictic Calendar NP
entry.pattern: NP[this/last/next + calendar noun or weekday] in temporal adjunct use

1.definition: Uses the contextual present to select an adjacent or current calendar period.

projection.target: The NP can be a time adjunct without on. The relevant Tuesday is selected by the deictic expression, with some variation in how speakers resolve next.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Next Tuesday, with no on
curious.summary: Words like this, last and next before a day or calendar period say when something happens, measured from now.
curious.body:
In I'll call next Tuesday, the phrase next Tuesday tells us when, and it needs no on in front. The word next picks out a Tuesday by counting from the present moment. This, last and next work this way.

Which Tuesday counts as next can vary between speakers, since it depends on how next is resolved. The context of the present is what fixes the period.
curious.try: Say I'll call next Tuesday. Which Tuesday do you mean? Ask a friend which one they would pick.

teacher.summary: Shows how this, last and next with a weekday or calendar noun give a time adjunct without on.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an NP made of this, last or next and a calendar noun or weekday, used as a temporal adjunct. It uses the contextual present to select an adjacent or current calendar period. The NP can be a time adjunct without on. The relevant Tuesday is selected by the deictic expression, and this dictionary notes some variation in how speakers resolve next. This dictionary relates it to month-and-day dates and to year names, and treats the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls the pattern a bare deictic calendar NP, where the time is picked out by the context of the present.

contrasts.note: A deictic NP used as a time adjunct, without on.

watch_for: A learner might add on before next Tuesday, when the NP can be a time adjunct without on.
A learner might assume next Tuesday picks out the same day for every speaker, when speakers resolve next with some variation.
teacher.activity: Fix a date on the board. Students say which day they take next Friday and last Monday to be from that date, and compare their choices.

child.hook: Does "next Tuesday" mean the same day for everyone?
child.explain: Words like this, last and next can go right before a day. I'll call next Tuesday. We don't need on. Which Tuesday next means can change from person to person.
child.play: Look at a calendar and find today. Say which day you think next Friday is. Ask a partner if they agree.
